Safeguards — documentation and content

Why published manuals are redacted, re-scanned and aborted on any leak, why the application serves no manual of its own but the console prints one offline, and the guards that stop a correct page from rendering blank.

👤 ForAdministratorAdvanced user
📍 WhereThe documentation publishing pipeline and the public website; satom show docs on a node
On this page
  • Documentation leaving the building
  • Content and presentation

Documentation leaving the building#

The internal manuals are written with real addresses, host names and node names, because that is what makes them useful to the operator. Publishing them is therefore a data-loss risk in the opposite direction: a published page is cached and indexed whether or not it is deleted afterwards.

Guard What it prevents
Redact, then scan the output, then abort A leak with a receipt. The publishing step rewrites known identifiers and then re-scans what it produced; a hit stops the build, naming the pattern, file and line. A warning inside a publishing pipeline would be a leak that was announced and shipped anyway.
Publication is opt-in A new manual being published by the mere act of existing. A document absent from the register is not published.
One rendered copy on the internet A second rendered copy running on a management server — which is exactly how an unauthenticated route once served internal addresses to anyone who could load the sign-in page. The application serves no manual itself; the sign-in page and the sidebar link to the published copy.
A single shared registry The generator and the application drifting into two different ideas of what is public. Both read one module, and the test suite fails if either re-declares the list, the redaction table or the scanner.
The scanner is tested against real input A round trip that proves nothing. Narrowing the redactor and the scanner together leaves the pair self-consistent and green while publishing the identifier, so a test asserts that the raw source still contains something the scanner must catch.
Placeholders that cannot vanish An invisible redaction. Angle-bracket placeholders were being parsed as unknown HTML elements and rendered as nothing, silently deleting a word from the sentence. Placeholders now use braces, which mean nothing in Markdown or HTML.
Product identifiers are deliberately not redacted Mutilating documentation without hiding anything. Workspace keys and URL segments are part of the product, not of anyone's estate. What is redacted is anything that helps someone reach a machine.
Manuals readable with no network A published-only manual being unreachable on an isolated management network. satom show docs prints any document straight to the terminal, which is what makes a single published copy safe.

ℹ️Note — The scanner is a backstop

The scanner recognises the identifier shapes it was built for. It protects against accident, not against someone deliberately describing a topology in prose. The opt-in register is the real control; the scanner makes forgetting expensive instead of silent.

Content and presentation#

A whole class of failure produces a perfect HTTP response, a complete document, a clean security scan — and a blank page. These guards exist because that happened.

Guard What it prevents
Content is visible by default A page that renders nothing when its script is blocked, stale or filtered. Hiding is applied by a blocking snippet in the document head, and only for the duration of the animation.
The hiding flag is withdrawn if the revealer never runs The inverse failure: the head arms the concealment and the script that would undo it fails to load. A timeout removes the flag.
Any visible pixel reveals a section A threshold expressed as a fraction of the element rather than the viewport. A document taller than about eight screens could never reach it, so the longest and most important manuals were the ones rendering at zero opacity.
Assets carry a content hash A visitor with fresh markup and a cached script — which reads as "this feature is broken", not "your cache is old". The hash is derived from the file, never from a version constant somebody can forget to raise.
The product icon is served on every surface A rebrand that never reaches the browser tab. The bare icon path is answered explicitly, because a browser requests it on its own and caches a 404 — a missing route is precisely why an old icon outlives a rename.
No live template serves the previous brand Assets whose file name mentions neither the old nor the new name, and which therefore survive every text search. One had outlived three renames on the first page shown after sign-in.

💡Tip — How this class is verified

These defects cannot be found by reading the HTML — the HTML was correct every time. They are verified by measuring the computed style in a real browser, on the real published pages.
